lede: A club weighs 18 fish and writes down a mean and a standard deviation. Then someone notices that one mass was copied down wrongly. Nobody is going to weigh the fish again, and the individual masses were never kept. Everything you need is still there, in two totals.
can: Recognise whether a question describes a correction, a removal or an addition
Rebuild $\sum x$ and $\sum x^{2}$ from $n$, the mean and the standard deviation
Adjust $\sum x$ by the values involved and $\sum x^{2}$ by their squares

md: The values may be gone, but the two totals behind the mean and the standard deviation can be rebuilt: $sum x$ from the mean and the count, $sum x^{2}$ from the deviation. Correct a value and $sum x$ moves by the difference, $sum x^{2}$ by the difference of the squares.

md:
A **correction** swaps one value for another: the count is untouched. A **removal** takes a value out and lowers the count by one. An **addition** puts one in and raises it by one.
Which of the three you are looking at decides what you divide by at the end, so name it before you calculate anything.

prompt: 18 fish were weighed and one mass is corrected. How many masses do you divide by afterwards?
explain: Still 18. A correction replaces a value; only a removal or an addition moves the count.

text: 2. Do not start again: adjust the totals

md:
You cannot edit a mean and you cannot edit a standard deviation, but you can edit a total. So rebuild both:
$\sum x = n\bar{x}$ and $\sum x^{2} = n\left(\sigma^{2} + \bar{x}^{2}\right)$.
For the weigh-in that gives $\sum x = 16920$ and $\sum x^{2} = 16698600$, and those two numbers now hold everything the original data held.

title: Why two totals are enough
md: The mean needs only $\sum x$ and $n$; the standard deviation needs only $\sum x^{2}$, $\sum x$ and $n$. No other feature of the data appears anywhere in either formula, so a data set of any size is completely described, for these purposes, by three numbers.

prompt: $\sum x = 16920$, and the mass 655 should have been 745. What is the corrected $\sum x$?
explain: $16920 - 655 + 745 = 17010$. Both numbers move: one takes the wrong mass out, the other puts the right one in.

text: 3. Squares come out, squares go in

md:
The second total behaves the same way, with one difference that costs more marks than anything else in Unit 3: what leaves $\sum x^{2}$ is a **square**, and what enters it is a **square**.
$\sum x^{2} = 16698600 - 655^{2} + 745^{2} = 16824600$.
Adding the raw difference of 90 instead is the attempt examiners saw most often.

title: Classwiz How-To: Finding the Mean, Standard Deviation and Quartiles from a Frequency Table
why: The calculator route for checking a recomputed mean and standard deviation once the totals are fixed.

prompt: A value of 47 is removed from a set. By how much does $\sum x^{2}$ fall?
explain: $47^{2} = 2209$. Subtracting 47 would be taking the value out of the wrong total.

text: 4. A worked example, start to finish

md:
18 trout, mean 940 g, standard deviation 210 g; the mass 655 should have been 745.
**Step 1.** $\sum x = 16920$ and $\sum x^{2} = 16698600$.
**Step 2.** Corrected $\sum x = 17010$, so $\bar{x} = 945$ g.
**Step 3.** Corrected $\sum x^{2} = 16824600$.
**Step 4.** $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{16824600}{18} - 945^{2}} = \sqrt{41675} = 204.14$ g.

text: 5. Removing and adding: the count moves too

md:
When a value leaves for good, three things change: $n$, $\sum x$ and $\sum x^{2}$. When one arrives, the same three change the other way.
12 clay-pigeon scores with a mean of 58 lose the score 47: the totals fall to 649 and 38351, the count falls to 11, and the new mean is 59.

prompt: The remaining 11 shooters have $\sum x = 649$. What is their mean score?

text: 6. Which way should the answer move?

md:
Before you write anything down, predict the direction. Removing a value below the mean pulls the mean **up**. Removing the value furthest from the mean pulls the spread **down**.
A replacement at the mean adds nothing to the spread at all, so the standard deviation falls, here from 5 to 3.42. If your answer moves the other way, something has gone wrong before the arithmetic.

prompt: A score below the mean is removed from a set. Which way does the mean move?
options: Up, because the values left behind are all larger
Down, because the set is smaller
It stays the same, because only one value went
answer: Up, because the values left behind are all larger
explain: Taking something below the centre out of a set pulls the centre upwards. It is a free check on every answer in this topic.

title: You can now
md:
Tell a correction, a removal and an addition apart, and say which of them moves $n$.
Rebuild $\sum x$ and $\sum x^{2}$ from $n$, the mean and the standard deviation.
Adjust $\sum x$ by the values and $\sum x^{2}$ by their squares.
Recompute the mean with the right count, and put that mean into the formula.
Predict which way the mean and the spread should move, and use it as a check.

Tell a correction from a removal or an addition.
Rebuild $sum x$ and $sum x^{2}$ from $n$, the mean and the deviation.
Adjust $sum x$ by the values and $sum x^{2}$ by their squares.
Run the two formulae again on the new totals.

A two-part question worth about seven marks: the corrected mean for three, the corrected deviation for the rest. The first mark is the rebuilt $sum x$; the last is the deviation recalculated from the adjusted totals. Stuck: write the two totals as they were before the correction and adjust them one at a time.
